So, the Marcos Jr administration, through its permanent representative in the United Nations (UN), Mr. Manalo, is now lecturing the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) on the “efficient, consistent, transparent, and non-selective” application of international law?? Seriously??? And we’re supposed to believe the room is nodding in solemn agreement??? Funny!! 🤣😂

Let’s ask the obvious question no one in Malacañang, and these senators seem brave enough to ask: who, exactly, is supposed to listen to us?

A Security Council that includes China, a permanent member with veto power, and with allies in the UNSC, and allied countries across the Global South and BRICS, while the world watches the Philippines fail to discipline a junior coast guard officer who publicly blabbers, postures, and insults a sitting head of state of one of the permanent member states of the UNSC without remorse? An underling who freelances foreign policy, gets caught, and is then openly shielded, protected, even applauded, by the Palace and cheered on by political grandstanding senators??? Seriously?? 

Credibility in diplomacy is not earned by PowerPoint bravado or hashtag jingoism disguised as patriotism. It is earned by discipline, coherence, and command responsibility. 

When Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the Constitutionally mandated architect of foreign policy and Commander-in-Chief, Chief Executive, cannot or will not rein in or discipline a subordinate, what signal does that send to the UNSC, to ASEAN partners, or to the international community? 

That the country’s foreign policy and diplomacy are crowd outsourced? 

That Philippine statecraft is optional? 

That LOUD MOUTHS the like of this coastguard outrank institutions like the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), the Senate, and the Presidency of this republic?

And spare us the sermons from the palace and senators who NORMALIZE this fiasco and this UNBECOMING and “BASTOS” (RUDE) behavior and decorum of this coastguard in uniform. 
You don’t get to preach “rule of law” abroad while SUSPENDING IT AT HOME! 

You don’t get to demand respect from the Global South, from the members of the UNSC and the UN, while trivializing diplomacy into a domestic political theater. Political capital is not infinite; it evaporates when you confuse chest-thumping with statecraft.

So yes, the Philippines’ representative and the Marcos Jr. government can urge non-selectivity all they want. But the world is not deaf; it’s discerning. And right now, the Philippines looks like a country asking for credibility while refusing to enforce basic discipline within its own ranks, a lowly subordinate at that, even the President of the Republic can’t discipline for Christ’s sake! 

Mr. President, this is the moment of truth. Restore diplomatic dignity or confirm that freelancing underlings and their backers run the show. 

Fire the Coast Guard officer, reassert your authority over your subordinate even in this instance alone, and put foreign policy back where it belongs: in the hands of professionals, not provocateurs, and in the hands of the DFA. 

Or admit what everyone already suspects: that you are WEAK and under the thumb of the handlers of this coastguard, and let history record who blinked.

Duh! 🙄🙄🙄

More than two years since they convened to develop initial short-term measures to address the perennial problem of overcrowded jails and prisons in the country, justice system stakeholders are now shifting their focus to long-term reforms with the launch of the Second National Decongestion Summit on January 21, 2026, at the Manila Hotel.

Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo said the gathering, organized by the Justice Sector Coordinating Council (JSCC), serves as a platform to build on the numerous achievements of the first Summit conducted in 2023.

The JSCC is a coordinative body composed of the #SupremeCourtPH (SC), the Department of Justice (DOJ), and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG). 

Chief Justice Gesmundo highlighted key reforms under the Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2022-2027,  disclosing that the SC En Banc is now deliberating the inclusion of a provision on custodial hearings in the proposed revisions of the Rules of Criminal Procedure. 

He also discussed other reforms which contributed to positive results, with data from the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology showing that the national jail congestion rate was reduced by 10% in just four months. 

Despite encouraging outcomes, the Chief Justice emphasized that the SC still recognizes the need for all branches of the government to do more.
